_comment: Events that are random on both servers by nature, not a gap of any card: dropped from the event sequence and from the byte comparison like a known gap (same rule shape, known_gaps.py), counted in the report under `random`, and compared statistically by stats.py. The Rust capture tests drop the same lines (`capture_compare::masked_lines`).

rules.why: Monsters move at random on both servers (spawns and wanderers), so whether and when a neighbouring room's monster makes noise (`You hear movement to the north.`) differs by chance; the line comes with a prompt of its own. Kept out of the event sequence and the byte comparison, counted per side, and compared as a rate per minute by stats.py (`monster noise per minute`) in the m2 scenarios. The original scrambles one letter of each direction word with a backspace (`wA\x08est`), which the byte pattern allows.

In the m2 (statistical) scenarios, monsters spawn and wander at random on both servers (the spawn pass and the wander pass), so whether one arrives during a given step differs by chance: `A giant rat creeps into the room from nowhere.` (the data-driven arrival) or `X moves into the room from the north.`, each with a prompt of its own. Kept out of the event sequence and the byte comparison; stats.py compares the spawn rate (gated) and the walk-in rate (advisory). The data-driven texts are classified by the game-data patterns (`world_patterns`, world_json.py), so a wrong text stays an unclassified line and fails. Only for scenarios marked statistical: the m1 walks keep comparing arrivals event by event.
